catalog_quote: 3.1. Primary stress in monomorphemes. The basic primary stress pattern of Samoan is simple: a moraic trochee at the right edge of the word (Homer 2007a). Stress is on the last vowel if long, and otherwise on the second-to-last. Examples are given in (4), with parentheses enclosing presumed feet, and acute accent marking primary stress. (4) Basic primary stress pattern: moraic trochee at right edge ... la(vá:) 'energized' ... le(léi) 'good' ... (mánu) 'bird' ... ma(nó i) 'to smell good' ... Samoan primary stress is similar to Fijian (Dixon 1988; Schütz 1978, 1985), where, in Hayes's (1995) analysis, a word ends with a moraic trochee. In both Fijian and Samoan, there are no surface forms with a short final vowel and a long penultimate vowel (e.g., *[má:nu])—see Section 5. We will see a systematic set of exceptions to the basic pattern in Section 7. ... 3.3. Analysis of basic primary stres…
sweep_summary: Samoan (samo1305) is in the catalog as 'weight' on Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014 (right-edge moraic trochee: final if long vowel/diphthong, else penult), corroborated by Pratt 1893. Of the five swept titles, two are first-hand word-accent studies that could not be obtained: Condax 1990 'Locative accent in Samoan' (Oceanic Linguistics 29(1): 27-48, DOI 10.2307/3623203, JSTOR-only; priority high, because a locative-conditioned accent shift would refine the morphology note) and Schütz 2007 'Accent patterns for English loanwords in Samoan' (Benjamins CLL 30: 133-146, DOI 10.1075/cll.30.16sch, paywalled, no abstract exposed; priority medium). The other three are sentence-level prosody: Yu 2011 (NELS 39; fetched sources from the author's site and read) is about an absolutive H- boundary tone but its §2 states the word-stress rule verbatim and confirms the catalog; Calhoun 2015 (Lingua, closed, not read) and Calhoun, Clemens & Elfner 2017 (Glossa, gold OA but the site's Anubis bot-wall blocked every PDF URL from our machine; abstract read) concern focus marking and prosodic phrasing, silent on stress placement. Two on-disk Yu papers (Prosodic Typology III preprint §12.1.1; Formal Grammar 2017) were also read and confirm the coding, adding the aea/aoa VVV antepenultimate exception. Nothing read supersedes Zuraw et al. 2014; catalog record stands. Glottolog 631804 mis-lists the NELS 39 editors (Lima, Mullin, Smith) as co-authors of Yu 2011. All fetches and non-fetches.

new_statements.reading: Word stress is weight-sensitive: a bimoraic trochee at the right word edge, so primary stress on a final long vowel or diphthong and otherwise on the penultimate syllable; secondary stress on preceding trochees; an LH pitch accent marks the stressed mora. Identical to the catalog's 'weight' coding (final-if-heavy-else-penult). Based on the same UCLA fieldwork (2008-09) as Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014, so it is corroboration by a co-author, not an independent source.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014 eprint at the stated section/page (sec. 3.1, ms p. 6; sec. 7.1 for the diphthong exceptions), and the corroborating Pratt 1893 passage is verbatim at Grammar pp. 2-3 in the held archive.org text. The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, moraic trochee: final stress iff final V: or diphthongising ai/au/ei/ou, else penult; secondary trochees leftward) rests on the best available source - a dedicated 2014 Phonology article with instrumental f0 evidence - and two later open works by co-author Yu fetched sources now (Prosodic Typology III preprint ch. 12; FG 2017) restate exactly this rule and report that Mosel & Hovdhaugen 1992 p. 28 and Churchward 1951 pp. 9, 24 agree. Nothing found suggests a different coding; the unheld reference grammar would only add corroboration.

sources.citation: Yu, Kristine M. 2011. The sound of ergativity: morphosyntax-prosody mapping in Samoan. In Suzi Lima, Kevin Mullin & Brian Smith (eds.), Proceedings of NELS 39, 825-838. [Glottolog 631804 lists Lima, Mullin & Smith as co-authors; the PDF's author line is Kristine M. Yu (UCLA) alone.]
sources.quote: Samoan is an intonational language without lexically contrastive tone. Stress is quantity-sensitive, with long vowels and diphthongs counting as heavy, and the basic primary stress pattern aligns moraic trochees at the right edge (Zuraw et al. 2008), e.g. ma(líni) 'marine', (mànu)(má:) 'dove'. Describing the intonational system in terms of the autosegmental-metrical framework (Ladd 1996, i.a.), the default pitch accent that occurs in each content word is a LH rise over the mora receiving primary stress (Orfitelli and Yu 2008), and declaratives end in utterance final low tones.
sources.locator: §2 'A brief overview of Samoan prosody', p. 2 of the PDF (txt ll. 60-70)
sources.note: The paper is about a high boundary tone (H-) at the left edge of absolutive arguments (phrasal/morphosyntactic tone), but its one-paragraph prosody overview states the word-stress rule: quantity-sensitive, long vowels and diphthongs heavy, right-edge moraic trochee, i.e. final if long/diphthong, otherwise penult ((mànu)(má:) 'dove', ma(líni) 'marine'), with an LH pitch accent on the primary-stressed mora. Cites Zuraw, Orfitelli & Yu 2008 (AFLA XV talk), the precursor of the catalog's deciding source.

sources.quote: The basic stress assignment pattern observed in native monomorphemes can be described as primary stress on the penultimate mora and analyzed with inviolable constraints enforcing trochaic, bimoraic feet within a prosodic word, e.g., ("manu) 'animal', ("la:) 'sun', with the the head foot aligned to the right edge of the prosodic word, e.g., ma("manu) 'design', (­sa:)("moa) 'Sāmoa' (Zuraw et al., 2014), see also Churchward (1951, p. 9, 24) and Mosel and Hovdhaugen (1992, p. 28). Exceptions come from stress on the antepenultimate mora in diphthongization of /ai, au, ei, ou/ VV sequences and additionally /aea/, /aoa/ VVV sequences, e.g., ("mai)le, *ma("ile) 'dog' but ma("ela), *("mae)la 'hollow', ("mae)a, *ma("ea) 'get'; see Zuraw et al. (2014, §8) for further details and analysis.
sources.note: Primary stress on the penultimate mora (right-aligned bimoraic trochee), so final stress when the last syllable is long (("la:)); diphthongising ai/au/ei/ou and aea/aoa sequences give antepenultimate-mora stress; secondary stress from further trochees; loanword secondary stress avoids epenthetic vowels; some intra-speaker variation in loans (taiamita). Cites Zuraw et al. 2014, Churchward 1951, Mosel & Hovdhaugen 1992. Restates the catalog's rule and adds the VVV-sequence exception detail.

sources.quote: 'The basic primary stress pattern in LSmo (and Samoan) is moraic trochees' at the right edge - a computational formalisation of the Zuraw et al. 2014 generalisations; no new descriptive data.
sources.note: A finite-state comparison of foot-based vs syllable-based grammars for a simplified Samoan stress system (LSmo) built from Zuraw et al. 2014: right-edge moraic trochee (penult, or final if heavy) plus Fijian-style secondary stress and initial-dactyl effects in loans. Confirms the catalog rule; not an independent descriptive source.

sources.quote: This paper investigates the functions of prosodic phrasing in the Austronesian VSO language Samoan. Two types of sentences are investigated, exclusives (involving the particle na'o 'only') and equatives. ... It was found that post-verbal absolutives modified by na'o are usually not preceded by a phrase boundary, unlike unmodified absolutives which are consistently preceded by a high phrase tone (H-) (cf. Yu 2009). ... The preferred order of constituents in Samoan is rheme-theme, with a high phrase tone marking the end of the rheme.
sources.note: Abstract only: the paper is about prosodic phrasing (H- phrase tones, phrase breaks) and information structure, not word-stress placement. It is gold open access (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar: GOLD, CC-BY) but every glossa-journal.org URL, including the Crossref-registered PDF galley, returned the Anubis 'Making sure you're not a bot' page from our machine; DOAJ record 403; web.archive.org unreachable from our machine; not on LingBuzz.
